A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same legal-concept interpretation and evaluation framework. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, worked examples, prompts and appendices support comparison despite renaming and appendix renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original Legal Concept Entailment experiments, ablations, human evaluation and appendix analyses, including Tables 1–5 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds a Farui-plus comparison, alternative-evaluator results and a human drafting efficiency study.

M1.justification: ATRI is renamed ATRIE and presented as an interpreter plus evaluator, but both components already exist in v1. Exact-match retrieval, filtering and reason extraction, label balancing, interpretation generation and LCE inference remain unchanged. The bilingual prompts match after Appendix F becomes G.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Chinese legal-case domain, 16 concepts from 14 articles, and interpretation and LCE tasks. The concept lists and test-dataset statistics match in v1 Appendix G and v2 Appendix H. Added model, evaluator and efficiency experiments do not establish additional dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Section 6.5 and Table 5 add Farui-plus as an interpretation-generator comparator against Qwen2.5-72B. The existing main and cross-model comparator sets remain unchanged. Other legal LLMs listed in Table 12 are surveyed for availability and context length, without corresponding evaluated results.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce a shared 10k-token input cap for Farui-plus and Qwen, Qwen2.5-72B/32B as alternative consistency judges, and a drafting-cost study involving two experts and five interpretations. These supplement the retained evaluation protocol; they do not establish revisions or reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends the supplementary analyses to test specialist versus general-purpose interpreters, sensitivity to the consistency evaluator, and computational versus human drafting costs (Section 6.5; Appendices C.5, C.6 and D). These address distinct practical and evaluation-validity questions beyond the unchanged retrieval, case-content and interpretation-component ablations.

E5.justification: v2 first reports human inter-rater agreement, Spearman rho = 0.42, and evaluator-ranking correlations of 0.943 and 0.829 (Appendices E.2 and C.5). Both versions already specify three repeated predictions with majority-label selection. No increase in repetitions or new confidence intervals is reported.

E6.justification: Substantive new findings concern interpreter specialization, evaluator agreement and efficiency. Table 5 reports Macro-F1 of 65.51 for Farui and 68.45 for Qwen under the shared 10k-token cap; these are new-setting results. Table 11 adds alternative-judge scores and rankings. Appendix D reports filtering 13k cases using 3.6 A40 GPU hours at $1.50, alongside human drafting averaging two hours and $20 per interpretation. Section 4.2 revises the reported source-case imbalance from above 100:1 to above 10:1, and Section 5.2 adds 24.9% concept prevalence. Existing benchmark, ablation and human-rating values remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The formal interpretation and LCE task definitions retain the same inputs, binary labels and generated reasons. Neither version adds substantive mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs; the new correlations are empirical analyses.

C1.justification: The central claims of automated interpretation, automatic LCE evaluation and expert-comparable quality remain. v2 makes the abstract's quality claim more qualified by identifying an accuracy gap alongside comprehensiveness and readability advantages. It also asserts present efficiency assistance, whereas v1's abstract frames practical support as an implication.

C2.justification: The sample-size limitation changes from financial constraints to restricted public access to judgments, accompanied by broader applicability claims when sufficient cases exist. v2 adds explanations for choosing general-purpose models and substituting open-source evaluators. Its ethical discussion also introduces strong assurances that real-case use poses no serious additional risks because professionals verify interpretations, substantially changing the earlier caution about real-world use.

D1.justification: v2 adds typical input-length information, A40 resource measurements, legal-model availability/context specifications, and details about annotator qualifications, shuffled presentation and independent scoring. These disclose aspects of existing procedures without establishing that the original human evaluation changed. It also drops v1's explicit article-selection threshold of over 10,000 citing cases and the $300/$130 evaluation-cost disclosures.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through a Chinese legal-LLM discussion and availability/context survey, including InternLM-Law, ChatLaw, DISC-LawLLM and Lawyer LLaMA. It also adds doctrinal-methodology and judicial-use literature, including Barak, Dworkin, Smits and Liu and Li. The established contrast with expert-dependent interpretation approaches remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, preliminaries and much of the methodological and results prose are extensively rewritten. ATRIE and LCE terminology organize a clearer interpreter–evaluator narrative, section headings are revised, and appendix organization expands. This exceeds routine copyediting even though the underlying pipeline remains stable.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5, 11 and 12, expands Table 2's row labels, clarifies Table 1's caption, and relocates Table 2 and Figure 4. Existing figures and matched tables otherwise retain their visual content, with the overall two-column main text and single-column appendix design preserved.

improvement.justification: The controlled Farui comparison and alternative-evaluator analysis strengthen support for model and evaluator choices, while disclosed independent human scoring and inter-rater agreement make the evidence easier to assess. Extensive editing also clarifies the framework. These gains are limited by the small efficiency study, whose GPU-hour and human-time measurements do not directly establish faster completion, and by new real-world risk assurances unsupported by deployment tests. Overall, the revision provides useful incremental validation and transparency.
